posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md: I have found that if I use Glassex to clean my plates as the final step before coating, that I get no spots where the gelatin wants to run to or run away from on the glass. Nice coatings each time. Glassex is the blue fluid that can be bought in those plant spray bottles to quickly clean window glass.

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md: The US equivalent is Windex, but I'm not certain that it is chemically identical to Glassex. Windex has a mild ammonia smell.

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md: I remember Windex from when I lived in the US. I think it smells the same. But I also remember that for cleaning airplane windows we used another product that was non-ammonia based. We used to buy that at a store called pep Boys, I think. It's worth to give both a try. The good thing about our Glassex is that I have no extra procedures to do. The glass can be cleaned and used while the MBDCG heats up and used immediately.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md: Hans, what do you use to wipe the cleaner off the glass?

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md: I just use a clean dry towel. I don't have a laminar flow chamber. After drying the dust from the towel is blown away by the hair drier when I pre-heat the plate. Of course then I get new dust on the emulsion as it dries in my garage.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md: Possibly you could make a shallow box frame out of wood. Then use a fine window screen for the sides and top. Then after you coat your plates place the screen box upside down over you plates. It will allow the plates to dry while keeping out most dust.

posts.author: glajciorz
posts.content_md:
Welcome everybody !

I'm completely new to holography - for now I've been making stereophotos, some CGH's and one hand-drawn hologram.

But I'm going to try making little holograms with PFG-1 plates and 7 mW diode laser.

About cleaning plates - maybe our technique for cleaning quartz wafers (before photolitography) could be useful. Cleaning solution is "pirahna" - 1:1 vol. mix of 95-98% sulphuric acid and 30% hydrogen peroxide.

Acid added to peroxide (!). Good wentilation required.

The mixture heats up itself to about 110 deg. C and is ideal for removing anything organic (i.e. photoresist) from our wafers. Removal of 4 um photoresist layer takes about 10 s (when mixture is not heated and not stirred). When heated to 180 deg. C it eats pieces of paper instantly.

After cleaning I rinse wafer in DI water (about 1l/wafer) and blowing with nitrogen (5N), quartz surface becomes completely hydrophilic.

Hope it helps.

greetings

Adam

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md:
This piranha stuff is pretty scary, even WITH proper lab safety gear ....

[http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piranha_solution](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piranha_solution)

See also ref. 1 for further comments and a lab accident description

[http://yarchive.net/chem/piranha_solution.html](http://yarchive.net/chem/piranha_solution.html)

posts.author: glajciorz
posts.content_md:
Thanks for the link. Indeed the worst thing one can do is to mix pirahna with acetone, isopropanol etc. - checked it myself, fortunately not with pure acetone.

I didn't say the pirahna is safe - after 5 years of working with it I still feel the respect and I think it's as dangerous as HF - but it's extremely effective glass cleaner.

If one knows what he's doing it may be very helpful.

greetings

Adam
